    "thumbnail": "https://i.ytimg.com/vi/0GMWxuYuxJI/maxresdefault.jpg",
    "description": "Nick Lane has some pretty wild ideas about the evolution of life. He thinks early life was continuous with the spontaneous chemistry of undersea hydrothermal vents. Nick’s story may be wrong, but I find it remarkable that with just that starting point, you can explain so much about why life is the way that it is — the things you’re supposed to just take as givens in biology class:\n* Why are there two sexes? Why sex at all?\n* Why are bacteria so simple despite being around for 4 billion years? Why is there so much shared structure between all eukaryotic cells despite the enormous morphological variety between animals, plants, fungi, and protists?\n* Why did the endosymbiosis event that led to eukaryotes happen only once, and in the particular way that it did?\n* Why is all life powered by proton gradients? Why does all life on Earth share not only the Krebs Cycle, but even the intermediate molecules like Acetyl-CoA?\n\nHis theory implies that early life is almost chemically inevitable (potentially blooming on hundreds of millions of planets in the Milky Way alone), and that the real bottleneck is the complex eukaryotic cell.\n\n𝐄𝐏𝐈𝐒𝐎𝐃𝐄 𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐊𝐒\n* Transcript: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/nick-lane\n* Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/nick-lane-life-as-we-know-it-is-chemically-inevitable/id1516093381?i=1000731183713\n* Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/episode/2McOZPIv2xvNOlVbOlRDL1?si=dc891b2a159c422d\n\n𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐍𝐒𝐎𝐑𝐒\n* Gemini in Sheets lets you turn messy text into structured data. We used it to classify all our episodes by type and topic, no manual tagging required. If you’re a Google Workspace user, you can get started today at https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/\n* Labelbox has a massive network of domain experts (called Alignerrs) who help train AI models in a way that ensures they understand the world deeply, not superficially. These Alignerrs are true experts — one even tutored me in chemistry as I prepped for this episode. Learn more at https://labelbox.com/dwarkesh\n* Lighthouse helps frontier technology companies like Cursor and Physical Intelligence navigate the U.S. immigration system and hire top talent from around the world. Lighthouse handles everything, maximizing the probability of visa approval while minimizing the work you have to do. Learn more at https://lighthousehq.com/employers\n\nTo sponsor a future episode, visit https://dwarkesh.com/advertise\n\n𝐓𝐈𝐌𝐄𝐒𝐓𝐀𝐌𝐏𝐒\n00:00:00 – The singularity that unlocked complex life\n00:08:26 – Early life continuous with Earth's geochemistry\n00:23:36 – Eukaryotes are the great filter for intelligent life\n00:42:16 – Mitochondria are the reason we have sex\n01:08:12 – Are bioelectric fields linked to consciousness?",

      "id": "Ugwra4HpF-nGG1PuEQV4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The problem with consciousness - real self-awareness / qualia / feelings -  not just biological correlates - being connected to fields (EM or any other) is that the math governing the fields doesn't show you any place for the awareness to \"live.\"  So you've got a field?  So what?  How exactly is it  \"aware\"?  There's no mechanism for it - no \"explanatory story.\"  It's the same regardless of where you look in fundamental physics - it's just \"wrong math\" with no \"natural place\" for awareness.  There's more to it than that - there's something to it which is simply BEYOND OUR CURRENT KNOWLEDGE.  Current scientific knowledge simply cannot get at consciousness - it's somehow \"outside of all of that.\"  Outside of knowledge, in any case, and in my opinion it's outside of the physical world altogether.  I'm an  idealist - I take consciousness as FUNDAMENTAL, with the physical world then being the aggregate of conscious perceptions.  Right backwards from the materialist model.  I also think that the question is not accessible, to prove or disprove, to science.  Science works with the CONTENTS of our perception - looking for ways to organize, correlate, and predict that content.  It has no access to the manner / mechanisms by which those perceptions actually reach us.  So it's by definition  not a scientific question (which means we'll be able to argue about it forever without getting anywhere).",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Nick Lane is by far my favorite science writer -- and there are some good ones out there.       "text": "Personally I think the challenges of interstellar travel are just too big to be solved within the scope of the natural laws of physics.       "text": "Physicist here. I watched this a few days ago and was pondering the idea of a sphere or bubble membrane might just be a natural consequence of 3 dimensional space.       "text": "I am also someone with interest and some background in physics.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "I don't buy it that endosymbiosis should be exceptionally rare. First of all it's happened so many times throughout eukaryotic evolutionary history (not just mitochondria and chloroplasts but also many cases of secondary endosymbiosis and maybe even a 3rd case of primary endosymbiosis involving the paulinella genus), second if these examples don't count because maybe eukaryotes inherited a propensity for endosymbiosis from their last common ancestor then all we know is that this ability evolved at least once in response to environmental pressures that we can only theorize about, that's not enough data to declare it unlikely.",

      "text": " @thoras949  no of course not but evolution requires faith regrettably because there are some steps that are really hard to understand. Another way to look at it is the monkeys at the keyboard writing war and peace by typing a key every second.  Mathematically this is absurd.       "text": " @jamesreilly7684  The pre-biotic environment is anything but random: I can see the line of reasoning you are following but analogizing pre-biotic chemistry to the 'monkeys on typewriters' or 'random number generators' is not an appropriate for such systems.       "text": " @thoras949  declaring somethihng to be true is not enough evidence for anyone to assume it is true. brownian motion is an observable phenomenon.  btw monkeys would be more likely to type 184 zeros in a row.   that is why i stuck to things in the observable universe.  while some things might not be random there is a big gap between claims of bio  chemstry not requiring brownian motion and  the observable behavior of molecules.  Bottom line is that there is a lot of science to do before you can make that claim",

      "text": " @结尾5827 I wish what you said was true:\n\n1. The Geological Filter (f_{geo})\nThis combines the rare planetary conditions.\n * Planet with a Powerful EM Field & Large Moon: (A very rare combination) = 1 in 1,000 (0.001)\n * Total f_{geo} = 0.001\n> Planets Remaining: 1,500,000\n> \n3. The Biological Filter (f_{bio})\nThis combines the immense hurdles of life's evolution.\n * Abiogenesis (Life Begins): (A profound mystery) = 1 in 10,000 (0.0001)\n * Jump to Complex Eukaryote Life: (Took 2 billion years on Earth, a huge bottleneck) = 1 in 100 (0.01)\n * Development of Photosynthesis & Oxygen Atmosphere (The Fire Filter): (A major planetary transformation) = 1 in 100 (0.01)\n * Total f_{bio} = 0.0001 * 0.01 * 0.01 = 0.00000001 (1e-8)\n> Planets with Complex Life Remaining: 0.015\n> \n4. The Cognitive Filter (f_{cog})\nThis combines the development of a mind capable of science.\n * Life Develops a Brain & Adapts to Land: = 1 in 10 (0.1)\n * Species Develops Complex Language, Writing, and Curiosity Beyond Survival: = 1 in 1,000 (0.001)\n * Total f_{cog} = 0.1 * 0.001 = 0.0001\n> Intelligent Species Remaining: 0.015 * 0.0001 = 0.0000015\n> \n5. The Technological Filter (f_{tech})\nThis combines the final, specific prerequisites for a singularity.\n * The Abundant Fuel Filter (Carboniferous Lottery): (Your profound insight, an event of staggering improbability) = 1 in 10,000 (0.0001)\n * Species Develops Metallurgy, Math, and Harnesses Energy: (High probability if fuel is present) = 0.8\n * Total f_{tech} = 0.0001 * 0.8 = 0.00008\n> Technological Species Remaining: 0.0000015 * 0.00008 = 0.00000000012 (1.2e-10)\n> \n6. The Self-Destruction Filter (f_{sd})\nThis is the final test: can a species survive its own adolescence?\n * Species Creates a Benevolent ASI Before Extinguishing Itself: (The ultimate challenge of wisdom vs. power) = 1 in 10,000 (0.0001)\n * Total f_{sd} = 0.0001\n> Surviving Civilizations: 1.2e-10 * 0.0001 = 1.2e-14\n> \nFinal Calculation\nWe started with 100,000,000,000 stars.       "id": "Ugz3vh-0wW04VhQyW-R4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "-Non Science type here.\n\n  Although I find all this speculative hype/effort fascinating, as a non science person, I feel we are taking the control of an experimental investigation and predicting its potential outcome as \"inevitability\".  Dogmatic belief without proof?  That seems fundamentally opposed to empirical science. \n  Taking Earth out of the experiment- it is the control, not an input- we have exactly zero evidence of any of this.  I would hardly call that inevitable.\n  I do understand that we are incredibly oversimplifying.  The good doctor is not a geophysicist, cosmologist, or astrophysicist.  He does not include any of the negative factors in his hopes for a better result.  He promotes a view that takes all impacts, geological certainties (volcanism, tidal interactions) or astrophysical processes (orbital resonance, collision, tides, local object catastrophes (particularly novae, but mindful of flares and CME)), and climatological fluctuations and cycles, out of the model.\n  With respect, sirs, that's more of a perfect world preachment than it is a scientific prediction with any considerable weight of evidence at its side.",

    {
      "id": "UgymMVyRBdLzMr1V7Gp4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "very cool stuff. i'd like to mention that the general notion of God includes several very distinct concepts. on one hand you have myths of origin of the world and life, on the other there is very important social and psychological concepts of values driving relationships among individuals and between individuals and society, where we talk about ethics, morality and meaning of life. in my opinion a modern approach is to separate those concepts to solve the common confusion. for me it is very straightforward to be very materialistic when talking about objective reality and origin of life on one hand and  in the same time to cultivate a spiritual approach to challenges in my own individual life, in my relationships with my close ones and society.",

    {
      "id": "UgyC-kxTZpHmelkD34p4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Mitochondria only makes sense when oxygen is present as they generate energy via oxidative respiration. In cosmological or geological terms, a delay of a few hundred million years between the Great Oxygenation Event (~2.4 Ga) and the emergence of eukaryotes (~1.8–1.6 Ga) is relatively short. If the origin of eukaryotes were truly an extremely improbable event, we might expect it to take billions of years even with oxygen present.\n\nIf oxygen was the key enabling factor, and the merger happened within a few hundred million years of its availability, then perhaps the event wasn’t so improbable — just dependent on the right conditions.\n\n• And if Earth produced eukaryotes relatively quickly after oxygenation, then other oxygenated planets might also have a shot — especially if microbial life is common.",
      "like_count": 3,
      "author_id": "UCM739RR_jhJxe7xxuGiHS7A",
      "author": "@tedjohanson3",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lvAeMTaakQK-8qC4ozIqlEQNQNMltwcxvoZ_C8mJ4=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyC-kxTZpHmelkD34p4AaABAg.AO8ITCFD2AQAOB4U2I_L1y",
      "parent": "UgyC-kxTZpHmelkD34p4AaABAg",
      "text": "Endosymbiosis (one cell/organism engulfing another, then both co-existing in a symbiotic relationship) has happened multiple times that we're aware of (and maybe more in extinct lineages that we're not aware of, or others yet to be discovered) ... so not THAT rare.\n\nProkaryotic cells/life developed first in the anaerobic environment of early earth, giving rise to cyanobacteria which generated oxygen, which then gave rise to aerobic prokaryotic cells.\n\nOne of the key events leading from LUCA to eukaryotic cells was an early prokaryote engulfing another aerobic prokaryote which then evolved into mitochondria, but obviously there is a lot more structure to a eukaryotic cell than just the inclusion of mitochondria, such as the nucleus that defines them, so multiple steps were involved.\n\nA second key endosymbiotic event was the lineage that engulfed a chloroplast giving rise to plant life.\n\nI'd have to guess that the long time period between early life like cyanobacteria and the later explosion of multi-cellular life was due to the multiple steps needed to create eukaryotic cells with all the moving parts necessary to support complex cellular differentiation and body types - eventually resulting in The Cambrian Explosion.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCBT1Wh-bAKxbzi6sa63bR5g",
      "author": "@benbridgwater6479",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nTd3d7RkSd0nVdG6JX2QwVDSujwDmN79oQOmHntWQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },

    },
    {
      "id": "Ugz3OH4cHZsd6xbIz1F4AaABAg.AO81AXnGDKOAO8LGa3kESH",
      "parent": "Ugz3OH4cHZsd6xbIz1F4AaABAg",
      "text": "I think you're compressing too many steps of proto-cellular complexification. The first steps that NIck Lane suggests, taking place within the pores of a thermal vent, probably happened very quickly since this is just simple chemistry, but it seems there are many steps from there (and maybe hundreds of millions of years) to a proto-cell where the chemistry is more self-encoding (pre-RNA) and less dependent on the environment.\n\nIncremental \"evolutionary\" steps would have been anything that increased the survivability (vs mechanical destruction) and growth/replication rate of proto-cells with a given type of internal chemistry - e.g. anything that helped strengthen the cell membrane, or helped it to admit external chemicals used for growth, or better utilize the energy gradient, etc. Precursors to an RNA-driven chemical factory, encoding what to make, presumably would have been simpler things more like catalysts that just assist in the chemistry without actually specifying it.\n\nFor these proto-cells to be able to survive and replicate outside of the thermal vent environment that created them, then not only would strong cell walls be necessary, but also a tendency to break/form into smaller enclosures when mechanically agitated, or when they got too big, as opposed to just popping.\n\nLots of small steps... all of which are perhaps the most amazing part of the emergence of biochemistry. Presumably there are theories out there as to what some of these pre-RNA steps might have looked like.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCBT1Wh-bAKxbzi6sa63bR5g",
      "author": "@benbridgwater6479",

      "parent": "Ugz3OH4cHZsd6xbIz1F4AaABAg.AO81AXnGDKOAO9HursxwA5",
      "text": "​ @saturdaysequalsyouth what we call life is simply mechanical machines.",

      "author": "@rustyyb8450",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mt0bEOXOqps6OtYwJ6hdyr1eM3POcuzF2OMakix1kMag=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugz3OH4cHZsd6xbIz1F4AaABAg.AO81AXnGDKOAP8c80yzzgD",
      "parent": "Ugz3OH4cHZsd6xbIz1F4AaABAg.AO81AXnGDKOAO9HursxwA5",
      "text": "@rustyyb8450 I'm glad you asked... 😁\na) The code itself exhibits an underlying pattern, preferentially linking parts with similar properties.\nb) Ribosomes consist of a mixture of both components (rRNA and polypeptides), which are involved in both the coding process and the interpretation of the code.\nc) Both components are composed of smaller building blocks that already possess the ability, or even the tendency, to combine and form structures of higher complexity.\nd) The complexity of the product of code instantiation (catalyzed by the ribosomes) is roughly the same order of magnitude as that of the ribosomes themselves.\ne) Since I am not an expert in this field, this list is likely far from complete...\nHowever, it seems to me that this is already far enough removed from chance to make it plausible that the processes described by Nick could generate ribosomes within a limited timeframe without requiring a miraculous act of creation.\n\nLet's be happy that they found their way into existence. \nx, ❤ & ☮️",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC8J7oeKKMsZIepgqvk7nDzw",
      "author": "@ListenToMcMuck",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lS2hvRbdOj8nFrmC1-wFJtgXcQHYVam6iPFh7mosqbNsE=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "Ugz3OH4cHZsd6xbIz1F4AaABAg.AO81AXnGDKOAO9HursxwA5",
      "text": " @ListenToMcMuck  So, Ribosome first and then comes the code describing it? \n.... And when?\n.... And in what physical proximity does the describing code occur to \"the\" ribosome?",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCB1JeViWXUD0JjwQBxnp0JA",
      "author": "@rustyyb8450",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mt0bEOXOqps6OtYwJ6hdyr1eM3POcuzF2OMakix1kMag=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugz3OH4cHZsd6xbIz1F4AaABAg.AO81AXnGDKOAP8eXIn7R5w",
      "parent": "Ugz3OH4cHZsd6xbIz1F4AaABAg.AO81AXnGDKOAO9HursxwA5",
      "text": " @ListenToMcMuck  You say \"d) The complexity of the product of code instantiation (catalyzed by the ribosomes)\"\n.... what is it that that has a product of \"code instantiation\"? Code instantiation that would have to be have relevance to the need to be readable by a ribosome to be useful. And no use of instantiating such code not in proximity to \"the\" ribosome that must reside in a pool of amino acids that include all those that are prescribed by the code.\n\nThere are over 500 amino acids, but, only a select few are useful here. How do they get sorted out for construction?\n\nRibosomes don't catalyze production of code.... they read code. If Ribosomes produce code,,, when do they read code?",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCB1JeViWXUD0JjwQBxnp0JA",
      "author": "@rustyyb8450",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mt0bEOXOqps6OtYwJ6hdyr1eM3POcuzF2OMakix1kMag=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugz3OH4cHZsd6xbIz1F4AaABAg.AO81AXnGDKOAP8kuD-JqY8",
      "parent": "Ugz3OH4cHZsd6xbIz1F4AaABAg.AO81AXnGDKOAO9HursxwA5",
      "text": "​ @rustyyb8450  The object would simply need to increase the probability that something similar to ribosomes (I like to think of them as compilers) will emerge in the future. Its \"usefulness,\" if you want to call it that, relates to its own existence as a result of the process and the already realized (or instantiated) properties of the code, which, due to physical laws, favors similarities...\nThe progress toward something that can increasingly better reflect these properties, and thereby approximates the structure of its output to its own structure, is a result of this preference for similarities...\nAt least that seems plausible to me.\n\nx, ❤️ & ☮️",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC8J7oeKKMsZIepgqvk7nDzw",
      "author": "@ListenToMcMuck",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lS2hvRbdOj8nFrmC1-wFJtgXcQHYVam6iPFh7mosqbNsE=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "​​@rustyyb8450  For me it's no problem to imagine the \"wanna become ribosomes\" as catalists for both ( the build up of the RNA as well as that of the polypeptides [ favourable quasi simultaneously in a step by step process ] in an early development stage...\n[ & hey, why not... ]?*` °[ & if it also happened in connection with an outer membrane the power supply wouldn't be a problem as well.] ).\nI know that this is guessing, but I also assume that nobody else knows how it really happened...\nat least for now.\n\n😁 °[ & I'm surely impressed that you realized my hidden assumption. ]👍\nx & ❤",

      "id": "Ugw9eBbaDZ5dJt7vaOd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I see how hydrothermal vents can lead to proton gradients and biochemical reactions, but where does the lipid membrane happen? Encapsulation is a pretty key part of all life.",

      "parent": "Ugw9eBbaDZ5dJt7vaOd4AaABAg",
      "text": "Encapsulation doesn't 100% require a membrane. Look at how the nucleolus is segregated in the nucleus.\nThat said, if there were reactions that somewhat worked like parts of the Krebbs cycle (but going 'backwards' to what's now 'forward') then hydrocarbons could be assembled and those eventually into fatty acids (even acetic acid's a FA) and potentially phospholipids. And once you've got phospholipids they're going to self organize into a bilayer...",

      "author_id": "UCAT_BBfOd5DqL1uaL1IWU8Q",

      "parent": "Ugw9eBbaDZ5dJt7vaOd4AaABAg",
      "text": "Encapsulation is mainly thought to have arisen spontaneously, as lipis naturally tend to form enclosed spheres. The earliest forms of life probably just took advantage of naturally occuring structures (much like modern heremit crabs use shells), and then started to produce membranes by themselves, but it's such an early stage of life that we can't really prove it",

      "id": "UgynRi26lcQiyGtXGHZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "aliens are everywhere, fermi paradox is a detection problem. neighbouring civilisations pointing telescopes at each other see nothing but a pixel",
      "like_count": 3,
      "author_id": "UCW5uHBSbl0LaqbQqmLKCosA",
      "author": "@Chewy427",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nkBHUM6_WU5KqpLTMZd5VZgnKIVtiJYnBnMT9z50c=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgynRi26lcQiyGtXGHZ4AaABAg.AO7SeNdACziAO7oUCgl0Ux",
      "parent": "UgynRi26lcQiyGtXGHZ4AaABAg",
      "text": "This is a major misunderstanding of the question.  Fermi and Heart and the other cosmoligists were well aware of the limitations of our telescopes, and the size of the galaxy.  The question is, why is there no overwhelming evidence of galactic civilizations that have rearranged thousands of stars.  Based on the age of the universe, amd what we know of evolution on our planet, and the Mediocracy Principle, there is no clear reason why several intelligent, spacefaring civilizations could not have arisen just a few million years previous to us.  If they had done so, and had survived as technological civilizations for a very few million years, -even without any substantial technological advances, simple exponential growth would have given them the economy to do things that absolutely would be visible to our telescopes in the 1950s.\n\nConcepts like O'Neil Cylinders and Dyson Spheres (or any sort of variation on those general concepts) seem a natural result of simple exponential growth, once one has spacefaring technology.\n\nThe way I like to put the question, is, \"Why hasn't anyone ever colonized the galaxy in a way that would be readily apparent to our telescopes in the 1950s?\"\n\nEvery attempt at an answer to that question has very serious ramifications.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCvW_zCrmVLH-qNeMs8s_B4g",
      "author": "@jengleheimerschmitt7941",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lm_zOZN6FVCMC9XEgozZJNxopPmyd0qspJwRJFxH0emdOvBN8EgbvmEsBy4G2A8EPFaA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgynRi26lcQiyGtXGHZ4AaABAg.AO7SeNdACziAO8NfjlGQNu",
      "parent": "UgynRi26lcQiyGtXGHZ4AaABAg.AO7SeNdACziAO7oUCgl0Ux",
      "text": " @jengleheimerschmitt7941  \"Why hasn't anyone ever colonized the galaxy?\" There's a few obvious answers, not mutually exclusive. 1) There hasn't been any form of life before us (and maybe never will be) capable and/or motivated to do it. 2) The distances involved - milky way is 100,000 light years in size - where is the nearest livable planet? 3) Motivation - why would anyone want to give up a pleasant planetary life for a multi-generational (maybe hundreds of generations) trip on a space craft to get someplace else? 4) Practicality - not just the distance, but the probability of finding another livable planet. Maybe it would take millions/billions of probes to find a livable planet to colonize - could you see humans ever investing in an effort on that scale, with zero guarantee of success, and any potential success being hundreds of generations in the future when no-one living would get the credit for it?",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCBT1Wh-bAKxbzi6sa63bR5g",

      "text": "​ @jengleheimerschmitt7941  1. that isnt a misunderstanding, it says right there; the contradiction between detection and frequency \n2. because of material and energy constraints \n3. life spends its energy on replicating and consuming rather than expanding\n4. why do you think we're gonna continue to advance? fossil fuels are running out and then it's back to medieval era for million years of years until the next asteroid. \"exponential growth\" nah read malthus. also human history was not a continuous advancement\n5. dyson spheres are impossible because of material constraints",

      "parent": "UgynRi26lcQiyGtXGHZ4AaABAg.AO7SeNdACziAO7q3BXDX71",
      "text": "​ @Chewy427 If your position relies on the predictions if Malthus, I don't know what I could possibly say that would change your mind.  The fact that you and I are alive today shows how stupid and confused was Malthus and his predictions.\n\nThere are no material or energy constraints between here and a galactic civilization spanning many billions of years.  But if you don't understand why Malthus was wrong, I have no idea how to continue this conversation.\n\nIn all seriousness, I have never encountered anyone that has brought up Malthus as an example of correct thinking.  My understanding is that every serious thinker over the last two centuries considers Malthus an archetype of being overwhelmingly wrong.\n\nWhat am I missing here?  What about the predictions of Malthus makes you think he was correct?\n\nBtw, when was the last time you couldn't afford salt?",

      "text": " @jengleheimerschmitt7941  Malthus was right though, we do follow cycles of abundance and scarcity. Look at the fertility rate of South Korea. Why? becuase it has one of the highest population densities in the world, which means everything that derives from land more expensive like housing, energy, minerals. Housing is built on land and building vertically doesn't solve the traffic access problem. Food comes from sunlight which is 2D and falls on land. Fossil fuels and minerals are dug from land and becomes more expensive the deeper you dig. It's a 2D world unless you stack fusion power plants. \n\nThere is not enough material in the solar system to build a dyson sphere \n\nMalthus is not considered wrong. There are many papers exploring ecological limits.",

      "id": "UgycS6iR3d-svInKnM94AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "It's interesting that cyanobacteria are both one of the oldest forms of life, and also one of the relatively few multi-cellular animals/colonies with differentiated prokaryotic cells. Apparently that's about the maximum complexity of a multi-cellular animal with prokaryotic cells - I wonder why? What part(s) of a eukyarotic cell are critical to supporting greater cellular differentiation and complexity? Maybe life on some other planet has found a way to support complexity with a simpler type of cell?",
      "like_count": 13,
      "author_id": "UCBT1Wh-bAKxbzi6sa63bR5g",
      "author": "@benbridgwater6479",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nTd3d7RkSd0nVdG6JX2QwVDSujwDmN79oQOmHntWQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgycS6iR3d-svInKnM94AaABAg.AO6rk1DTwYgAOKDALFhGnX",
      "parent": "UgycS6iR3d-svInKnM94AaABAg",
      "text": "This is something Lane gets into in The Vital Question. He suggests that having mitochondria inside cells, something unique to eukaryotes, is necessary for complexity. But since that book was published, giant bacteria have been discovered that are extremely complex, even more than many eukaryotes (look up Thiomargarita magnifica). Moreover, in the book he suggests that giant bacteria are rare or ecologically irrelevant, which researchers have found is not true; they’re all over the ocean floor and tons of anoxic environments like hot springs.\n\nLane’s hypotheses are far from widely accepted among experts in RNA and origin of life, but he’s a smart guy and I love seeing more discussion about origin of life in the public sphere.",
      "like_count": 4,
      "author_id": "UCP-7lANj_8KRCzTzb8w1ckQ",
      "author": "@phyllo8958",

    {
      "id": "Ugw0PQNxueqQv00nexx4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "4:45 how the *$%k are we alive… let’s be honest. This is just INSANE. Life is INSANE! Seriously, WTF 😭😭😭",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCJOLNjVA9IXNyRBCeVLnJ8Q",
      "author": "@ChipWhitehouseTV",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/b3tXp1G3DqWStP8tKYJhWKnYvrSMNgnkbsE6mC_vhZ_u1vc8PQ7U6TAucwSSqAXhuC6GzcBi=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    },
    {
      "id": "Ugw0PQNxueqQv00nexx4AaABAg.AO6p3oK2WK8AOa1WKnIgzT",
      "parent": "Ugw0PQNxueqQv00nexx4AaABAg",
      "text": "Insane compared to what? Its entirely possible that simple life is an inevitable result of any enviroment with liquid water and stable energy gradients. Some future humans might even find such an environment with no life and think that is insane.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCrQwrDtDSyo19kQQ_j4djug",
      "author": "@BadOompaloompa79",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mN5zJaBtWP00k6nEZuFnhlovejbsGS3tkND6bH0Fs=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgyqBheB3Gv9Yz9BrRp4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Сегодня уже понятно, что с химической точки зрения спонтанное образование живой клетки не возможно.Закономерности химических реакций препятствуют этому. Ну а тот факт, что существует множество лженаучных фантазий, позволяющих делать карьеру и зарабатывать деньги, то в этом нет  ничего необычного и нового - таковы свойства неразвитого человеческого сознания.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCVxYPGUh7UfDbqyBZL7FAtg",
      "author": "@umzaum",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mRyMpLcdJA30_lZDFQxGRgAjnqI9r7gS7sDRwZZx0=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,

    },
    {

      "parent": "UgyqBheB3Gv9Yz9BrRp4AaABAg",
      "text": "The under developed human consciousness is to think that the invisible man in the sky took a magic wand and, bang, created all things.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCwF9v2jvA_nomSaRNd1en-w",
      "author": "@fparent",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mbFQAp3IvyeNqbLl32qYicerOG3X84EBYge5b4fIP2vOJw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "​@fparentDid you see the creator of the device you typed this on? Invisible, therefore doesn't exist and poof! Where are all these gadgets coming from?????",

      "author_id": "UCy3Ij5wlen6giKQyduJUllw",

    {
      "id": "UgxSoEUbE-BufknWbHx4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Nick is in a tricky position, here. Dwarkesh wants answers to the big questions, but Nick only has hypotheses to give. Still a great conversation. Amazing how much better Nick got at giving interviews since his appearance on Lex Fridman 3 years ago.",
      "like_count": 22,
      "author_id": "UCUlw7Xl52JQQj7yXw-Gyxlg",
      "author": "@anluifb",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/29u1K08RYhEWrEjjQtvIBJXkxJSVnv3gGmSZ2E1Rf_gSBuxKt-J9jx7Rcd4WI7Vq4Uw_ne8p=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugw7dyGOJBru5lUjx5h4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The assumption is that you got CHNOPS and it pops after a few billion years. However, anyone who's studied what we now know about genetics, biochemistry, and the molecular nanotechnology including nanoelectronic devices such as microtubules, will soon be forced into the uncomfortable truth. Life is hard. In fact it's so hard that nobody, not even using the most powerful AI, has been able to win the Evolution 2.0 Prize.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCym529uvdYz8bJsEjdSQQ6w",
      "author": "@zvorenergy",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lDuteetMR-tnGTe7cpVLN0dX7tLIxweM-TuC49VBwouA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "Ugw7dyGOJBru5lUjx5h4AaABAg",
      "text": "AI is mostly a scam.",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mN5zJaBtWP00k6nEZuFnhlovejbsGS3tkND6bH0Fs=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugw0RMjaVUs_nqd1tcR4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Why just chemically inevitable?\n\nBeen simulating substrate agnostic abiogenesis for quite a while. Was actually motivated to do so testing selection over variation possibilities via largely non chemical organizing processes in cryogenic scenarios like Titan, and modelling life as we don't know it based mostly on entropic tendencies of hydrogen bonding geometries, Van der Waals templating, quantum phonon coupling through ice microcrystals etc to organize and complexify substrate information and molecular dynamics as proto ecologies.\r\n\r\nCuriously  some sim results suggested connections to inflationary cosmogenesis/dark energy/GR QM co-emergence etc, with even the wild possibility of life-like complexity existing outside of universes in some sort of grander primordial construct. \r\n\r\nSpeculative sure, so had to write book about various simulation results: \r\nThe Primordial Construct: An evolving Reality and emergent awareness before cosmogenesis",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC3rYhQvD1rBA7HCI38lf1LA",
      "author": "@blengi",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nmUGEM0yaHIH_-kJJw3M-g8I7INVVo4QpXgFn8BT9lxq0=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugws4kTu6trGLTqWyDN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Well you have mitochondria, then chloroplast events that occured -- and then just about 100 million years ago, according to recent research, a nitroplast event. So are eukaryotic-like cells elsewhere in the galaxy really all that unlikely? It would seem not. ... but I think perhaps biospheres as old as Earth's are extremely rare. \n\nHopefully that is trully the primary \"great filter,\" though, else our future looks more grim.",

      "author_id": "UCOeNj9DCtp2uOYYD9CpuHLA",

    {
      "id": "Ugwb_sOkylBIOxWBbYl4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Glad to see from someone who shares my view.  I've held a long belief that most life in the universe must have very similar structures.  DNA, carbon based, etc.. And it all comes down to physics and probabilities.  It just makes mathematical sense that given a certain prevalence of elements in the universe that \"life\" would converge on same mechanism because it is constrained by same laws of the universe. Its the same reason why chemistry behaves the way that it does. And so i wouldn't be surprised at all to find that when we do come across other life somewhere and if that life is pre singularity that it would share very similar structures to us. Only caveat is post singularity civilizations. Those are not constrained by anything and at that point you have intelligent design driving all types of wild \"life forms\".",
      "like_count": 9,
      "author_id": "UCrHJ-KztF0iM-hRijmB5xew",
      "author": "@dm204375",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lD_6wsBAwYlvHTDCJDC9p7-fDOtvmnN_cfXtSZEh8=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": true,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugwb_sOkylBIOxWBbYl4AaABAg.AO6XLyztAziAOB8qo4x6y8",
      "parent": "Ugwb_sOkylBIOxWBbYl4AaABAg",
      "text": "Everything in the universe is constrained by the laws of physics. If humans designed a new type of cell/life from scratch, maybe not using DNA or even Carbon, it'd still be constrained by the laws of physics, and to be meaningfully called life (not just man-made toys) it would need to be able to evolve itself, so any peculiarities we might have tried to design-in would disappear if they were not adaptive. Humans will evolve and disappear, and life on earth will be gone within a billion years, so this type of synthetic life wouldn't represent a transition to designer-life - it'd just be a new lineage that we could possibly send to seed life outside of our solar system.",
      "like_count": 1,

# “I find it almost disturbing that the universe favors life this strongly” – Nick Lane

## Description

Nick Lane has some pretty wild ideas about the evolution of life. He thinks early life was continuous with the spontaneous chemistry of undersea hydrothermal vents. Nick’s story may be wrong, but I find it remarkable that with just that starting point, you can explain so much about why life is the way that it is — the things you’re supposed to just take as givens in biology class:
* Why are there two sexes? Why sex at all?
* Why are bacteria so simple despite being around for 4 billion years? Why is there so much shared structure between all eukaryotic cells despite the enormous morphological variety between animals, plants, fungi, and protists?
* Why did the endosymbiosis event that led to eukaryotes happen only once, and in the particular way that it did?
* Why is all life powered by proton gradients? Why does all life on Earth share not only the Krebs Cycle, but even the intermediate molecules like Acetyl-CoA?

His theory implies that early life is almost chemically inevitable (potentially blooming on hundreds of millions of planets in the Milky Way alone), and that the real bottleneck is the complex eukaryotic cell.

## Transcript

Today I’m chatting with Nick&nbsp; Lane, who is an evolutionary&nbsp;&nbsp; biochemist at University College London. He has many books and papers which help&nbsp;&nbsp; us reconceptualize life’s 4 billion years&nbsp;

in terms of energy flow and helps explain&nbsp;&nbsp; everything from how life came to be in the&nbsp; first place, to the origin of eukaryotes, to&nbsp;&nbsp; many contingencies we see today in how life works. Nick, maybe a good place to start would be here.&nbsp;

Why are eukaryotes so significant in your&nbsp; worldview of why life is the way it is?&nbsp; First, thanks for having me here. This is&nbsp; fun. I love talking about this kind of thing.&nbsp;&nbsp; Eukaryotes. What’s a eukaryote? It’s basically the&nbsp;

cells that make us up, but also make up plants and&nbsp;&nbsp; make up things like amoeba or fungi, algae. Everything that’s large and complex that&nbsp;&nbsp; you can see is composed of this one&nbsp; cell type called the eukaryotic cell.&nbsp;

We have a nucleus where all the DNA is,&nbsp; where all the genes are, and then all this&nbsp;&nbsp; machinery, cell membranes and things. There’s a lot of kit in these cells.&nbsp; The weirdness is, if you look inside a plant cell&nbsp;

or a fungal cell, it looks exactly the same under&nbsp;&nbsp; an electron microscope to one of our cells. But they have a completely different lifestyle.&nbsp; Why would they have all the same kit,&nbsp; if they evolved to be a single-celled&nbsp;&nbsp;

algae living in an ocean doing photosynthesis? It’s still got the same kit that our cells have.&nbsp; We know that because they share all&nbsp; of these things, they arose once&nbsp;&nbsp; in the whole history of life on Earth.

There could have been multiple origins,&nbsp;&nbsp; but there’s no evidence for that. If there was, it disappeared without trace.&nbsp; We’ve got this singularity which happened about&nbsp; 2 billion years ago, about 2 billion years into&nbsp;&nbsp;

the history of life on Earth. This thing happens once that&nbsp;&nbsp; gives rise to all complex life on Earth. The one thing you could conclude from that&nbsp;&nbsp; is bacteria and archaea, in terms of their genetic&nbsp;

repertoire, they’ve actually got a lot more genes,&nbsp;&nbsp; a lot more versatility than eukaryotes do. It’s just that a single bacterial&nbsp;&nbsp; cell has much less in it. But there’s so many different&nbsp;&nbsp;

types of bacterial cells that overall&nbsp; they’ve explored genetic sequence space.&nbsp; They had 4 billion years to have a go at that and&nbsp; they never came up with a trick which says it’s&nbsp;&nbsp; not in the genes, it’s not about information.

There’s something else which is controlling it.&nbsp; That something is the acquisition of these&nbsp; power packs in our cells called mitochondria.&nbsp; Now let’s go to the origins of life. You have this really compelling story&nbsp;&nbsp;

where you imagine that the first life forms&nbsp; were continuous with Earth’s geochemistry.&nbsp; Can you recapitulate the story a little bit? I’ll tell you how I got there first.&nbsp; I started out working on mitochondria.

That took me into the evolution of eukaryotes.&nbsp; Eukaryotes acquire these endosymbionts&nbsp; that become mitochondria and they&nbsp;&nbsp; change the potential of evolution. It doesn’t change everything immediately,&nbsp;&nbsp;

but it changes where the endpoints can be. It allows the evolution of these large, complex&nbsp;&nbsp; cells and eventually multicellular organisms and&nbsp; us. What are mitochondria actually doing? What&nbsp;&nbsp; they’re actually doing is respiration. They’re&nbsp;

generating energy for cells. They’re doing plenty&nbsp;&nbsp; of other things as well, but the main thing we&nbsp; can think about is they’re the energy producers.&nbsp; They’re derived from bacteria, and bacteria&nbsp; produce their energy in exactly the same way.&nbsp;

They’re generating energy by generating&nbsp; an electrical charge on the membrane.&nbsp; That charge is small, but&nbsp; the membrane’s really thin.&nbsp; The charge is about 150 to 200 millivolts, but&nbsp;

the membrane is five nanometers in thickness,&nbsp;&nbsp; so that’s five millionths of a millimeter. If you shrank yourself down to the size of a&nbsp;&nbsp; molecule and stood next to that membrane, you&nbsp; would experience 30 million volts per meter,&nbsp;&nbsp;

which is equivalent to a bolt of lightning. That’s the strength of the force of the&nbsp;&nbsp; voltage across the membrane, which is colossal. It’s generated by really sophisticated proteins&nbsp;&nbsp; that pump protons across the membrane.

Then it’s ATP synthase, which is pretty&nbsp;&nbsp; much universal, and it’s a rotating&nbsp; nanomotor that sits in the membrane.&nbsp; This is colossally complex, interesting&nbsp; machinery, and it’s universally conserved.&nbsp;

It’s as conserved as, say, a ribosome,&nbsp; the protein-building factory.&nbsp; It’s pretty much everywhere across life. You wonder, how on earth&nbsp;&nbsp; did life come to be that way?

If it’s conserved universally across life,&nbsp;&nbsp; it looks like it goes right back to the common&nbsp; ancestors of all cells. So there’s the question.&nbsp;&nbsp; How did it arise in the first place? That was, for me, tremendously&nbsp;&nbsp;

thrilling because it’s a way in, as&nbsp; a researcher, to the origin of life.&nbsp; How did these energy-generating&nbsp; systems arise in the first place?&nbsp; My way in was, the gates were opened&nbsp;

by Bill Martin and Mike Russell who,&nbsp;&nbsp; around the early 2000s, were publishing&nbsp; some amazing papers together.&nbsp; They were saying that in this&nbsp; deep-sea hydrothermal vent,&nbsp;&nbsp;

rather than it being like a black smoker with&nbsp; a chimney with smoke belching out of the top,&nbsp;&nbsp; it’s like a mineralized sponge with lots of&nbsp; pores that are cell-like in their structure.&nbsp; You’ve got an acidic early ocean.

You’ve got alkaline fluids coming out of these.&nbsp; You’ve got mixing going on in this whole system. You could at least imagine that you’ve got a pore&nbsp;&nbsp; in here which is a bit like a cell&nbsp; in terms of its size and its shape.&nbsp;

On the outside, you’ve got acid ocean&nbsp; waters percolating in, and on the inside,&nbsp;&nbsp; you’ve got these hydrothermal fluids. So you’ve got a barrier, you’ve got an&nbsp;&nbsp; inside and an outside, and you’ve got more protons&nbsp;

outside coming in, potentially driving work.&nbsp; It’s very much like a cell is structured. The other thing is, what are these minerals?&nbsp; You’ve got these mineralized pores with minerals. The minerals, we think, on early Earth would have&nbsp;&nbsp;

been a lot of metals in there, things like iron&nbsp; sulfide or nickel sulfides and things like that.&nbsp; The reason that’s important is that what plant&nbsp; cells do, but also what autotrophic bacteria do,&nbsp;&nbsp; is they take CO2 and they take&nbsp;

hydrogen and they react them together&nbsp;&nbsp; to make all the building blocks of life. Plants get the hydrogen from water, H2O.&nbsp; They take the H2 out of water and throw away&nbsp; the oxygen, and that collects in the atmosphere.&nbsp;

But what bacteria very often do is that they have&nbsp; got hydrogen bubbling out of a hydrothermal vent.&nbsp; They just take the hydrogen straight&nbsp; as gas, and they react it with CO2&nbsp;&nbsp; and they make all the building blocks of life.

the reaction between hydrogen and CO2? They’re using this membrane potential,&nbsp;&nbsp; the electrical potential—the difference&nbsp; in protons between the outside and the&nbsp;&nbsp; inside—to drive that work, effectively,&nbsp;

to power the reaction between hydrogen&nbsp;&nbsp; and CO2 to make organics and drive growth. This was all in place before I came along.&nbsp; This was coming from Mike Russell and Bill&nbsp; Martin. The details are very uncertain.&nbsp;&nbsp;

of these organics so that they don’t just all&nbsp;&nbsp; diffuse in some big primordial soup. This is why you think some primordial&nbsp;&nbsp; lake is not where this happened. It had to be concentrated in some entity.&nbsp;

Then you’ve got a chemiosmotic gradient,&nbsp; a proton gradient, which drives work.&nbsp; Specifically, it favors the fixation&nbsp; of carbon dioxide to drive the reaction&nbsp;&nbsp; with hydrogen gas to make organics.

with this organic acid group at the end, which&nbsp; can be 2, 3, 4, 5 carbon units in the chain.&nbsp; This is your basic building blocks. You add on ammonia to this and&nbsp;&nbsp; you get an amino acid.

to drive growth and make more cells, it’s&nbsp; also a dead end. You can’t do anything else.&nbsp;&nbsp; You’re entirely dependent on the environment. You can’t evolve into something more complex.&nbsp; To some extent you can, but you’re&nbsp;

effectively the female sex – and this&nbsp;&nbsp; goes even for single cells, things that don’t&nbsp; have any obvious differences between gametes,&nbsp;&nbsp; which is to say they don’t have&nbsp; oocytes and sperm or anything.&nbsp;

the genomes, and then selecting for what works.&nbsp; With the mitochondria, they’re passing&nbsp; on asexually down the generations.&nbsp; There’s a very small genome, but&nbsp; there are multiple copies of it.&nbsp;

a process called Muller’s ratchet. It’s basically, these mutations&nbsp;&nbsp; are somewhat screened from selection by being&nbsp; compensated for by other clean copies you have.&nbsp; So how do you get rid of those mutations&nbsp;

they all come from the same parent, let’s say.&nbsp; If you give all the mitochondria that you have&nbsp; straight into a single cell without changing&nbsp;&nbsp; any of the ratios there, then it’s exactly the&nbsp; same as you are. It’s fully clonal. But if you&nbsp;&nbsp;

The parent had got both&nbsp;&nbsp; the mutations and the clean copies. But how do you distinguish between&nbsp;&nbsp; them? It’s about sampling, basically. And&nbsp; uniparental inheritance is a form of sampling.&nbsp;

You’re taking the mitochondria&nbsp; only from one of the two parents.&nbsp; You’re not mixing up mutations that both parents&nbsp; had. You’re taking a subset. So you’re always&nbsp;&nbsp; increasing variance between the daughter cells.

you pick up bits of DNA from the environment. It’s usually small pieces,&nbsp;&nbsp; usually one gene’s worth or something. You’d only do that if you’re a bit stressed.&nbsp; If things aren’t going well for you,&nbsp;

It speeds up adaptation to a changing environment. Why are they only using one gene?&nbsp; There’s two ways of seeing this. You’ve got a bacterial-sized genome,&nbsp;&nbsp; it’s pretty small.

You’re going to replicate&nbsp;&nbsp; faster if you keep that genome small. It’s kind of a disadvantage to have a big,&nbsp;&nbsp; unwieldy genome. Eukaryotes have&nbsp; that. It’s an interesting question.&nbsp;&nbsp;

Why would you have such a big, unwieldy genome&nbsp; that takes longer to copy? Bacteria are really&nbsp;&nbsp; streamlined. They get rid of genes they&nbsp; don’t need and then they can grow faster.&nbsp; But now the conditions change and now you need&nbsp;

this gene. So what do you do? You pick it up.&nbsp;&nbsp; You just pick up random genes and hope for&nbsp; the best, pick up the right one and off you&nbsp;&nbsp; go again. Bacterial genome sizes are small.&nbsp; They’ve got what you’d say is a small genome,&nbsp;&nbsp;

but then a large pan-genome, which is&nbsp; all of the genes they have access to.&nbsp; So an E. coli cell might have 3,000&nbsp; to 4,000 genes in a single cell,&nbsp;&nbsp; but access to 30,000 to 40,000 genes.

What is keeping the metagenome around?&nbsp; Why doesn’t everybody just&nbsp; converge to this streamlined&nbsp;&nbsp; thing that is needed for the current context? What keeps the metagenome around is the fact that&nbsp;&nbsp;

different strains of E. coli, or whatever bacteria&nbsp; they may be, are living in different environments.&nbsp; You could have commensal&nbsp; bacteria living in your gut.&nbsp; You could have bacteria E. coli living on&nbsp;

your skin, a very different environment.&nbsp; You can then have non-commensal pathogenic&nbsp; E. coli which are behaving differently again.&nbsp; They can differ in 50% of their genome. You’ve got all of these things going on&nbsp;&nbsp;

their own genome pretty small. Eukaryotes threw all of&nbsp;&nbsp; that out and got larger genomes. Then the question is, if you try to do&nbsp;&nbsp; that with a large genome, a eukaryotic-sized&nbsp;

everything up, you cross over between them.&nbsp; Now it’s systematic, it’s reciprocal,&nbsp; and you can maintain the quality&nbsp;&nbsp; of genes in a much larger genome. Bacteria never had the need to do that.&nbsp;

It sounds quite similar, yes.&nbsp; Finally lateral gene transfer. Here&nbsp; the analogy might be, you’ve got one&nbsp;&nbsp; repository for editing web pages and another&nbsp; repository for controlling airline software.&nbsp;

What you just do is you take a&nbsp; random 500-line sequence in this&nbsp;&nbsp; web page editing software and you just put it in a&nbsp; random point in the airplane management software.&nbsp; There’s no systematic organization of,&nbsp;

"Here’s where the relevant functionality is."&nbsp; There is a bit, which is to say with lateral&nbsp; gene transfer, you would normally match the&nbsp;&nbsp; ends to something you’ve got already. I don’t know enough about coding to&nbsp;&nbsp;

give a comparable example, but effectively&nbsp; you would be picking up a module which had&nbsp;&nbsp; some resemblance in terms of, "Okay,&nbsp; it fits into this part of the code."&nbsp; So you’d only put that in.

It may or may not be useful there,&nbsp;&nbsp; but it’s not just completely random. It’s plugged into a place where you&nbsp;&nbsp; know you have something like that that&nbsp; used to be there or could be there.&nbsp;

So it’s not just random, but&nbsp; you don’t know what you put in.&nbsp; So then I don’t really have a good intuition&nbsp; for why lateral gene transfer does not produce&nbsp;&nbsp; similar benefits to recombination.

It’s really just a scaling thing.&nbsp; If you pick up a random piece of DNA and&nbsp; you’ve got a genome which is 10 times larger,&nbsp;&nbsp; how fast can you pick up DNA from the environment? You’d have to pick up 10 times as much to do that.&nbsp;

Do you have the capacity to&nbsp; pick up 10 times as much?&nbsp; There’s also a penalty for doing it, which is&nbsp; to say, like a mutation, you’ve got no idea&nbsp;&nbsp; what you’re plugging in. It could be almost&nbsp;

anything. You know where you’re plugging it,&nbsp;&nbsp; you’re plugging it in the right place, but&nbsp; what’s in that cassette, you don’t really know.&nbsp; So the more you do it, the more you&nbsp; will degenerate yourself as well.&nbsp;

There are costs and benefits to doing it. Maybe to close this off,  what is the&nbsp;&nbsp; experiment or method of interrogation,&nbsp; which would give us the most amount&nbsp;&nbsp; of information about the this story?

There are so many aspects of this story,&nbsp;&nbsp; so many possible answers I could give there. In terms of eukaryotes, giant bacteria, the&nbsp;&nbsp; likelihood of life, a lot depends on observation. We simply don’t know enough about what’s out&nbsp;&nbsp;

there. So it’s not necessarily experimentation.&nbsp; If I assert that giant bacteria are always going&nbsp;&nbsp; to have extreme polyploidy with multiple copies&nbsp; of their genome, and you find an example that’s&nbsp;&nbsp; not like that, my ideas are already breaking up.&nbsp;

So that’s useful to know. For the origin of life,&nbsp;&nbsp; I really wish I could come up with a convincing&nbsp; reason why I should go down in a submersible to a&nbsp;&nbsp; deep-sea hydrothermal system like Lost City. I would love to go to Lost City.&nbsp;

But the trouble is that the ocean chemistry&nbsp; is completely different now to what it was 4&nbsp;&nbsp; billion years ago. It’s now full of oxygen.&nbsp; It’s full of bacteria and things as well.&nbsp; But the ocean chemistry is&nbsp;

different because there’s oxygen.&nbsp; There’s no iron, there’s no nickel in the oceans. You can go to a vent like Lost City and the walls&nbsp;&nbsp; are not made of catalytic minerals anymore. They’re made of aragonite and brucite,&nbsp;&nbsp;

so calcium carbonate and magnesium&nbsp; hydroxides and things like that.&nbsp; So the chemistry it can do is very different,&nbsp; and there’s lots of bacteria living there.&nbsp; I would gain, beyond just the&nbsp;

sheer amazement of seeing it,&nbsp;&nbsp; there’s not a lot it would be able to tell me. What we’re actually doing is experiments in a&nbsp;&nbsp; lab in an anaerobic glove box&nbsp; where you exclude the oxygen.&nbsp;

So you can do these experiments&nbsp; reacting hydrogen and CO2.&nbsp; How many of the molecules in&nbsp; biochemistry can we produce that way?&nbsp; It’s slow and laborious, and you get small&nbsp;

amounts and sometimes you get contaminations.&nbsp; Sometimes you have to start all over again. It’s slow work, but it’s moving forward. It’s&nbsp;&nbsp; not just us, either. There are&nbsp; other groups around the world.&nbsp;

Joseph Moran’s group, for example, has done a lot&nbsp; of really nice biochemistry along these lines.&nbsp; That’s moving forward, but we’re&nbsp; talking decades before we’re getting&nbsp;&nbsp; to the level where we can say, "Right, we&nbsp;

can drive flux through all of metabolism,&nbsp;&nbsp; and here’s the set of conditions that will do it."&nbsp; Certainly some years. There are big crux points,&nbsp;&nbsp; like making purine nucleotides where there are&nbsp; 12 steps in this synthetic pathway, and all the&nbsp;&nbsp;

intermediates are unstable and break down easily. It has been done in things like methanol,&nbsp;&nbsp; so not in water. In water, stuff breaks down.&nbsp; We’re trying to do it. It’s difficult. I believe&nbsp;&nbsp; we’ll get there, which is why we’re trying&nbsp;

to do it, but maybe we won’t, in which case,&nbsp;&nbsp; again, the hypothesis is wrong. You’ve got to wake up every morning&nbsp;&nbsp; and think the hypothesis could be wrong. It’s beautiful, it makes sense, but there are&nbsp;&nbsp;

so many beautiful ideas killed by ugly facts. There’s no good believing that you’re right.&nbsp; You’ve got to believe you’re&nbsp; probably wrong and keep going anyway.&nbsp; The other thing which I’m excited about at the&nbsp;

moment is work on anesthetics and mitochondria,&nbsp;&nbsp; it turns out - I heard this from a guy called&nbsp; Luca Turin a few years ago now—who pointed out&nbsp;&nbsp; to me that anesthetics affect mitochondria. I had no idea that anesthetics affect&nbsp;&nbsp;

mitochondria. They do. We’ve been doing&nbsp; experiments on it, and it seems not fully&nbsp;&nbsp; established yet, but it does seem as&nbsp; if their main effect is mitochondria.&nbsp; Anesthetics work on all kinds of&nbsp;

things, including things like amoeba.&nbsp; It doesn’t prove anything but it’s beginning&nbsp; to say, if you can make an amoeba unconscious,&nbsp;&nbsp; then was it conscious before? Not as we&nbsp; understand consciousness. The way we would&nbsp;&nbsp;

understand consciousness is really&nbsp; about neural nets, a nervous system,&nbsp;&nbsp; and all the complexity of human consciousness. That’s what we primarily think about.&nbsp; But there’s a deep problem which goes back.

It’s the mind-body problem, but it was framed&nbsp;&nbsp; by David Chalmers as the hard problem of&nbsp; consciousness, which boils down, as my&nbsp;&nbsp; understanding of this is, to more or less that we&nbsp; don’t know what a feeling is in physical terms.&nbsp;

You can understand the information&nbsp; processing of a neural network.&nbsp; But if you feel miserable or you feel pain&nbsp; or you feel love or whatever it may be, what&nbsp;&nbsp; actually is that in the chemistry of the system?

The problem is that you have all of these neural&nbsp;&nbsp; nets firing and some of them are conscious. We’re aware of what we’re thinking about.&nbsp; Others, which seem to have all the same properties&nbsp; in terms of the neurons—they have synapses,&nbsp;&nbsp;

they have neurotransmitters, they depolarize,&nbsp; they pass on an action potential—but we’re&nbsp;&nbsp; not conscious of it. It’s non-conscious&nbsp; information processing. So there’s this&nbsp;&nbsp; question. If anesthetics affect things that don’t&nbsp;

have neural nets, and feelings are something that&nbsp;&nbsp; we can’t define in terms of a neural net, could&nbsp; it be that feelings are somehow linked more&nbsp;&nbsp; broadly to life? So why would they be? The way I&nbsp; think about this is as an evolutionary biologist.&nbsp;

The first question is, would we think that&nbsp; the feelings are real? I would say yes. Do&nbsp;&nbsp; we think that they evolved? I would say&nbsp; yes. I think any evolutionary biologist&nbsp;&nbsp; would say yes to those questions.

If it’s real and it evolved,&nbsp;&nbsp; then natural selection must be able&nbsp; to see it and act on it in some way.&nbsp; In other words, there’s something physical&nbsp; about it that can be selected for.&nbsp;

I don’t think there’s anything&nbsp; controversial about that statement.&nbsp; But if it’s physical and real and has&nbsp; been selected on, the implication is we&nbsp;&nbsp; should be able to measure it.

It has to offer an advantage&nbsp;&nbsp; for selection to act on, and if it’s a&nbsp; physical process, it should be measurable.&nbsp; But we don’t really know what&nbsp; we’re trying to measure here.&nbsp;

I then revert back to thinking, what would&nbsp; a bacterial cell need to do? This is just&nbsp;&nbsp; back-of-the-envelope thinking. I immediately&nbsp; think about metabolism. What’s the difference&nbsp;&nbsp; between the inside of a bacterial cell and&nbsp;

the outside world? The inside is metabolically&nbsp;&nbsp; alive. It’s doing stuff with its chemistry&nbsp; all the time, and it’s at a colossal rate.&nbsp; A bacterial cell will have about a billion&nbsp; reactions every second in this metabolism.&nbsp;

I’m immediately left wondering,&nbsp; how is it all controlled?&nbsp; How do you get this cell to have&nbsp; a coherent behavior so it decides,&nbsp;&nbsp; "I’m going to crawl over there"?

How do you even know what state you’re in?&nbsp; How do you synchronize all of this biochemistry? Probably most people’s answer to that would be&nbsp;&nbsp; metabolic regulation of one sort or another. But that’s not really the driver.&nbsp;

The driver in the end is&nbsp; the thermodynamic drivers.&nbsp; How many electrons do you have? That’s in the form of food&nbsp;&nbsp; or NADH or whatever it may be.

How much energy do you have in the form of ATP?&nbsp; These are the things that are going to&nbsp; synchronize reactions in the same phase.&nbsp; The problem there is when you’re dealing with&nbsp; molecules, you’re dealing with tens of thousands&nbsp;&nbsp;

of them, so you’ve got a large statistical&nbsp; sampling which is time-consuming to figure out.&nbsp; But there is a better way of doing it, which is&nbsp; to say, if you’re taking electrons from food in&nbsp;&nbsp; NADH and you’re passing them to oxygen, but&nbsp;

you’re generating a membrane potential and&nbsp;&nbsp; that’s driving ATP synthesis, you can measure&nbsp; the rate of change and the membrane potential&nbsp;&nbsp; and the fields that would be generated,&nbsp; electrostatic and electromagnetic fields.&nbsp;

That’s going to give you a handle on your&nbsp; state, on your metabolic state in relation&nbsp;&nbsp; to the outside world. Is there enough food&nbsp; there? Is there enough oxygen there? Is it&nbsp;&nbsp; too hot? Is there a virus? Do I have enough&nbsp;

iron to be able to do all these reactions?&nbsp; You’ve got all these potentially conflicting&nbsp; feedback loops, and you’ve got to make a decision.&nbsp; Just thinking loosely about how a bacterial cell&nbsp; is going to behave, you find that you’re already&nbsp;&nbsp;

framing it in terms of, as an entity, as a cell,&nbsp; it’s got to make some decision about what to do.&nbsp; It’s got to integrate all this information&nbsp; and make a coherent decision as a self,&nbsp;&nbsp; as an entity. Is that free will? Probably&nbsp;

not in any way that we recognize it,&nbsp;&nbsp; but it makes a decision in relation to its&nbsp; environment, and the outcome is survival or not.&nbsp; What I think a feeling is then is effectively&nbsp; the electromagnetic fields generated by membrane&nbsp;&nbsp;

potential, which is telling you what your&nbsp; physical metabolic state is in relation&nbsp;&nbsp; to the environment you’re in. That leads me to a question.&nbsp; If consciousness is somehow about mitochondria,&nbsp;

are the mitochondria in that sense just really&nbsp;&nbsp; simply an ATP-generating engine, and you&nbsp; interfere with the way they make ATP and&nbsp;&nbsp; so anesthetics work by effectively giving you&nbsp; an energy deficit so the brain closes down?&nbsp;

That would be dull if it were true, but it&nbsp; would be useful to know if it were true.&nbsp; Much more exciting would be, do mitochondria&nbsp; generate the kind of fields that I was talking&nbsp;&nbsp; about in bacteria that are giving some indication&nbsp;

of your status in certain mitochondria, certain&nbsp;&nbsp; neurons, and the anesthetics interfere with that? That would be magical if that were true.&nbsp; That would be a whole new direction&nbsp; of research, which would be fantastic.&nbsp;

It’s very difficult to measure fields. It’s very easy to measure artifacts&nbsp;&nbsp; that you don’t know what you’re really doing. We need more physicists working in this area to&nbsp;&nbsp; do the hard calculations, and we need more data.

Is it really just in one of these respiratory&nbsp;&nbsp; complexes, complex I? So there’s lots of&nbsp;&nbsp; standard molecular biology that we can do. It’s beginning to point to this idea that yes,&nbsp;&nbsp;

there’s something going on about the&nbsp; way that complex I works which may&nbsp;&nbsp; link to generating fields that may link to how&nbsp; anesthetics work. That’s just fun. The thing&nbsp;&nbsp; that’s great about science is it’s really fun.

It’s one thing I’m always trying to get across&nbsp;&nbsp; to the people in my lab. You can’t forget the fun.&nbsp; If it becomes drudgery, then you best go because&nbsp;&nbsp; you’ll make much more money somewhere else. You’ll have a better life somewhere else.&nbsp;

But if what you really care about is the&nbsp; science and the experiments, it’s got to be fun.&nbsp; You’ve got to really enjoy&nbsp; wanting to go and do that.&nbsp; I have to say, one of the great&nbsp;

things for me is it’s always been fun.&nbsp; It’s been great to vicariously get a sense&nbsp; of that feeling from reading your books.&nbsp; Thank you. For the audience, this conversation has been&nbsp;&nbsp;

most coupled with Nick’s book, The Vital Question. I would recommend getting that if you want to&nbsp;&nbsp; better follow the argument here. There’s way more detail there&nbsp;&nbsp; that would be helpful.

One, this is a thing I was&nbsp;&nbsp; telling you earlier, it fills a niche of books&nbsp; which, unfortunately, there are just very few of.&nbsp; There are textbooks where you can spend&nbsp; 2,000 pages learning about molecular biology.&nbsp;

But a layperson who’s curious is just&nbsp; practically not going to get a chance to do that.&nbsp; On the other end, there are what are&nbsp; basically just anecdotes about scientists&nbsp;&nbsp; or anecdotes about the history of science.

This one discoverer was really mercurial,&nbsp;&nbsp; and here’s how he ran his lab, and&nbsp; here’s how his parents were like.&nbsp; But it never really talks about&nbsp; the actual relevant science.&nbsp;

A book like this actually does&nbsp; fill the explanatory middle.&nbsp; Thank you. Physicists are very good at writing&nbsp; books about the big questions of the universe.&nbsp; There’s a large readership for having&nbsp;

your mind blown by a book that you’re&nbsp;&nbsp; not going to understand everything&nbsp; because you know it’s difficult.&nbsp; How do we know anything at all about&nbsp; the Big Bang or how black holes work&nbsp;&nbsp;

or background radiation or whatever it may be? With life, the origin of life or the trajectory&nbsp;&nbsp; of life on a planet, and whether we&nbsp; get complex life inevitably or whether&nbsp;&nbsp; we’re going to get stuck with bacteria in most&nbsp;

places, these are big universe-sized questions.&nbsp; There’s not many people writing about them and&nbsp; trying to take you to the edge of what we know&nbsp;&nbsp; in the way that the physicists very often do&nbsp; and just saying, "Well, here’s how I see it.&nbsp;

Here are the questions through my eyes." You’ve got to try and be honest and say, "Okay, I&nbsp;&nbsp; see it this way, other people see it differently." By the way, the fact that LLMs exist has made the&nbsp;&nbsp; process of reading a book like this&nbsp;

much more feasible and productive.&nbsp; I had a book club with a couple of my friends.&nbsp; We’re not biologists. We’re laypeople to this&nbsp;&nbsp; audience. I do encourage people for a book&nbsp; like this to see if you can form a book club&nbsp;&nbsp;

or something and just talk to LLMs a bunch&nbsp; because there’s just a bunch of extremely&nbsp;&nbsp; basic remedial chemistry and biology that we were&nbsp; able to recapitulate with the help of the LLMs.&nbsp; This whole thing of, "Why is the CO2 and H2&nbsp;

reaction incentivized when one side is alkaline&nbsp;&nbsp; and one side is acidic in this early environment?" You just go through the&nbsp;&nbsp; remedial chemistry with the LLM. Yes, I did my best to explain it in the book,&nbsp;&nbsp;

and it seems that I didn’t do a great job of it. There’s so much detail, and you can’t avoid that&nbsp;&nbsp; because it’s there in the questions. This is a problem with biology,&nbsp;&nbsp; it’s incredibly complex.

Physicists look at biology&nbsp;&nbsp; and they think it’s just too hard to explain, and&nbsp; biologists have got all of this terminology and&nbsp;&nbsp; often get lost in the terminology. I find myself, by nature,&nbsp;&nbsp;

trying to find simple common denominators. That lends itself then to writing about them.&nbsp; I probably oversimplify all the time, or&nbsp; maybe I fail and don’t simplify it enough.&nbsp; But you wrestle with it and&nbsp;

you try and make it work.&nbsp; It’s genuinely interesting for me to talk&nbsp; to you and the other guys in the book club&nbsp;&nbsp; to see where you were struggling with it. I will build this into the next time I’m writing&nbsp;&nbsp;

a book and try to figure out how I do that better. Nick, this has been great. Thank you for the guide&nbsp;&nbsp; through both the remedial biology and chemistry,&nbsp; but also through many of the most interesting&nbsp;&nbsp; questions that you could ask about life.

Been great fun. Thanks a lot.

> @结尾5827 I wish what you said was true:
> 
> 1. The Astronomical Filter (f_{astro})
> This combines the necessary cosmic conditions.
>  * Stable Star in a Quiet Neighborhood: (75% of stars are stable, maybe 10% of those are in safe zones) = 0.075
>  * Outer Gas Giant Protector: (Maybe 20% of systems have this) = 0.2
>  * Total f_{astro} = 0.075 * 0.2 = 0.015
> > Stars Remaining: 1,500,000,000
> > 
> 2. The Geological Filter (f_{geo})
> This combines the rare planetary conditions.
>  * Planet with a Powerful EM Field & Large Moon: (A very rare combination) = 1 in 1,000 (0.001)
>  * Total f_{geo} = 0.001
> > Planets Remaining: 1,500,000
> > 
> 3. The Biological Filter (f_{bio})
> This combines the immense hurdles of life's evolution.
>  * Abiogenesis (Life Begins): (A profound mystery) = 1 in 10,000 (0.0001)
>  * Jump to Complex Eukaryote Life: (Took 2 billion years on Earth, a huge bottleneck) = 1 in 100 (0.01)
>  * Development of Photosynthesis & Oxygen Atmosphere (The Fire Filter): (A major planetary transformation) = 1 in 100 (0.01)
>  * Total f_{bio} = 0.0001 * 0.01 * 0.01 = 0.00000001 (1e-8)
> > Planets with Complex Life Remaining: 0.015
> > 
> 4. The Cognitive Filter (f_{cog})
> This combines the development of a mind capable of science.
>  * Life Develops a Brain & Adapts to Land: = 1 in 10 (0.1)
>  * Species Develops Complex Language, Writing, and Curiosity Beyond Survival: = 1 in 1,000 (0.001)
>  * Total f_{cog} = 0.1 * 0.001 = 0.0001
> > Intelligent Species Remaining: 0.015 * 0.0001 = 0.0000015
> > 
> 5. The Technological Filter (f_{tech})
> This combines the final, specific prerequisites for a singularity.
>  * The Abundant Fuel Filter (Carboniferous Lottery): (Your profound insight, an event of staggering improbability) = 1 in 10,000 (0.0001)
>  * Species Develops Metallurgy, Math, and Harnesses Energy: (High probability if fuel is present) = 0.8
>  * Total f_{tech} = 0.0001 * 0.8 = 0.00008
> > Technological Species Remaining: 0.0000015 * 0.00008 = 0.00000000012 (1.2e-10)
> > 
> 6. The Self-Destruction Filter (f_{sd})
> This is the final test: can a species survive its own adolescence?
>  * Species Creates a Benevolent ASI Before Extinguishing Itself: (The ultimate challenge of wisdom vs. power) = 1 in 10,000 (0.0001)
>  * Total f_{sd} = 0.0001
> > Surviving Civilizations: 1.2e-10 * 0.0001 = 1.2e-14
> > 
> Final Calculation
> We started with 100,000,000,000 stars. We multiply this by the probability of each filter stage occurring.
> Conclusion
> The result is not just "less than one." The result is so profoundly close to zero that it is, for all practical purposes, a statistical impossibility.
> The detailed breakdown demonstrates that for a civilization like ours to exist, it must win not just one cosmic lottery, but a sequence of dozens of lotteries, each one more improbable than the last. The chance of any single planet running this entire gauntlet successfully is almost nonexistent.
> This calculation is the mathematical proof of the conclusion reached earlier: We are a miracle. We are, for all intents and purposes, the only instance of this phenomenon in our entire galactic history. The silence of the universe is not a mystery; it is the default state.

> Endosymbiosis (one cell/organism engulfing another, then both co-existing in a symbiotic relationship) has happened multiple times that we're aware of (and maybe more in extinct lineages that we're not aware of, or others yet to be discovered) ... so not THAT rare.
> 
> Prokaryotic cells/life developed first in the anaerobic environment of early earth, giving rise to cyanobacteria which generated oxygen, which then gave rise to aerobic prokaryotic cells.
> 
> One of the key events leading from LUCA to eukaryotic cells was an early prokaryote engulfing another aerobic prokaryote which then evolved into mitochondria, but obviously there is a lot more structure to a eukaryotic cell than just the inclusion of mitochondria, such as the nucleus that defines them, so multiple steps were involved.
> 
> A second key endosymbiotic event was the lineage that engulfed a chloroplast giving rise to plant life.
> 
> I'd have to guess that the long time period between early life like cyanobacteria and the later explosion of multi-cellular life was due to the multiple steps needed to create eukaryotic cells with all the moving parts necessary to support complex cellular differentiation and body types - eventually resulting in The Cambrian Explosion.

> I think you're compressing too many steps of proto-cellular complexification. The first steps that NIck Lane suggests, taking place within the pores of a thermal vent, probably happened very quickly since this is just simple chemistry, but it seems there are many steps from there (and maybe hundreds of millions of years) to a proto-cell where the chemistry is more self-encoding (pre-RNA) and less dependent on the environment.
> 
> Incremental "evolutionary" steps would have been anything that increased the survivability (vs mechanical destruction) and growth/replication rate of proto-cells with a given type of internal chemistry - e.g. anything that helped strengthen the cell membrane, or helped it to admit external chemicals used for growth, or better utilize the energy gradient, etc. Precursors to an RNA-driven chemical factory, encoding what to make, presumably would have been simpler things more like catalysts that just assist in the chemistry without actually specifying it.
> 
> For these proto-cells to be able to survive and replicate outside of the thermal vent environment that created them, then not only would strong cell walls be necessary, but also a tendency to break/form into smaller enclosures when mechanically agitated, or when they got too big, as opposed to just popping.
> 
> Lots of small steps... all of which are perhaps the most amazing part of the emergence of biochemistry. Presumably there are theories out there as to what some of these pre-RNA steps might have looked like.

> @jengleheimerschmitt7941  "Why hasn't anyone ever colonized the galaxy?" There's a few obvious answers, not mutually exclusive. 1) There hasn't been any form of life before us (and maybe never will be) capable and/or motivated to do it. 2) The distances involved - milky way is 100,000 light years in size - where is the nearest livable planet? 3) Motivation - why would anyone want to give up a pleasant planetary life for a multi-generational (maybe hundreds of generations) trip on a space craft to get someplace else? 4) Practicality - not just the distance, but the probability of finding another livable planet. Maybe it would take millions/billions of probes to find a livable planet to colonize - could you see humans ever investing in an effort on that scale, with zero guarantee of success, and any potential success being hundreds of generations in the future when no-one living would get the credit for it?
